grades.quote: If processor 1 executes thread A and processor 2 executes thread B, after a while each cache will hold the corresponding thread’s values. If the scheduler later schedules each thread on the opposite processor, most memory accesses will miss in the local cache and need to use the cache coherence protocol to retrieve data from the other cache.
grades.reason: The caption directly explains that after a thread runs on a processor, its data sits in that processor's cache. If the scheduler moves the threads to the opposite processors, most memory accesses miss in the local cache and must use the cache coherence protocol to fetch data from the other cache.
The passage is about zero-filling page frames and cache pollution. It says nothing about moving threads between CPUs.

grades.quote: As soon as one processor wants to write into the cache block, however, some communication between the caches is necessary so that other processors don’t read out-of-date values. Most typically, the cache where the writing occurs invalidates all the other caches’ copies so that it has exclusive ownership.
grades.reason: The passage gives background on cache coherence: writes invalidate other caches' copies, and blocks move between caches. That is related to why cross-processor cache traffic is costly. It is about spinlocks and does not cover thread migration.
The passage covers page placement policy and conflict misses in set-associative caches. It does not address thread migration between CPUs.
